The diseases include scrapie in sheep and goats, "mad cow" disease in cattle, and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) in humans. The word "prion" is derived from "proteinaceous infectious particle." Prions are small protein-containing particles with no detectable nucleic acid; they were suspected of being viruses, but they did not match any known viral characteristics. It has been shown that the prion protein (PrP) is encoded by the host's chromosomal DNA. Four major types of pain-relieving drugs are used in obstetrics: opioids, sedatives, epidural analgesia, and local anesthetics. All four can be safely administered during pregnancy and lactation and have proved effective in controlling labor pain.

Systemic opioids easily cross the placenta and are present in breast milk. However, their use has been associated with neonatal respiratory depression. Fetal exposure to these metabolites may cause neonatal seizures. Codeine and hydromorphone are less commonly used.
In contrast to systemic opioids, neuraxial opioids (intrathecal or epidural) do not readily cross the placenta or enter breast milk in clinically significant amounts. Therefore, they appear to be the preferred opioid agents for relieving labor pain while minimizing the risk of neonatal respiratory depression. These drugs are especially useful when the early stages of labor are prolonged and when patients desire epidural analgesia. Benzodiazepines are the class of drug most frequently chosen for this purpose. Diazepam and midazolam are the most common drugs used--midazolam is now used almost exclusively.
